To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the evolution of mammalian gene regulatory networks is shaped by endogenous retrovirales (ERV) that have been inserted in mammalian genomes over the last 100 million years.
endogenous retroviruselements have played a major role in the diversification and maintenance of mammalian immune gene regulatory networks.
the immune system is a copy and paste gene network, and that this copy and paste gene regulation is mediated by the evolutionarily ancient and ubiquitous ERVs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of endogenous retroviruselements in the evolution of the mammalian immune response, and in particular, the evolution of the major histocompatibility complex.
understanding how the evolution of gene regulatory networks (GNs) contributes to the evolution of phenotypic novelty and the origin of species.

the evolution of gene regulatory networks (7) The evolution of gene regulatory network architecture has been a major focus of evolutionary biology for decades, and has been the focus of intense interest for many years, especially with respect to understanding the evolution of development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the authors have shown that the ERVs have contributed to the regulation of immune genes.

the authors have shown that the ERV-derived regulatory elements in the human genome have a role in controlling the expression of genes in the immune system, and this role may have evolved from the role played by ERVs in controlling viral gene expression in retroviruses.

the authors have provided strong evidence that a copy-and-paste mechanism, involving ERV integration, has contributed significantly to the evolution of a large number of genes involved in the mammalian immune response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the immune system evolved by the insertion of retrovirus-derived regulatory sequences into the genome, and that these retrovirus-derived sequences are still active in the immune system of humans today.
we have shown that ERVs are a major source of new regulatory elements in mammalian genomes that are capable of driving the evolution of complex gene regulatory networks.
we show the importance of endogenous retrovirals as a source of cis regulatory elements for gene expression in mammalian genomes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of GRNs is more complex than previously appreciated, and that the evolution of regulatory systems controlling immune function in mammals is a particularly interesting example.
the evolution of GRNs is not necessarily a gradual, stepwise process.
